Looking for something to watch this weekend? Netflix UK just dropped 44 new movies and series, and there's a little something for everyone!

Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki star in 'Guarding Stars', a new romance about a bodyguard going undercover as a heartthrob's girlfriend. Also added: gripping Korean crime thriller 'The Blue Road' and 'Steps', a fun animated spin on the Cinderella story starring Ali Wong.

Which holiday movies are Netflix subscribers actually hitting play on? We dove into the official Engagement Reports covering 2023 through 2026 to rank the 50 most-watched Christmas movies on the platform. 

Illumination's 'The Grinch' leads the pack with a staggering 224 million views, followed closely by the high-stakes holiday thriller 'Carry-On'. Our list covers everything from animated specials to the classic rom-coms that keep fans coming back every December.
Netflix removing #GilmoreGirls: A Year in the Life next week isn't the end of the road for the miniseries ❤️

'The Beast in Me' is officially back in production! Filming for Season 2 is now underway in New York, and Netflix has announced some massive additions to the cast.

Riley Keough is joining as a series regular, while Aaron Paul boards the crime drama as a recurring guest star. They will be acting opposite returning stars Claire Danes, John Goodman, and Lili Taylor.
#TheDiplomat season 5 has an early filming update that suggests the longest wait between seasons yet 😬

Millie Bobby Brown and Jack Innanen will star in the upcoming Netflix romantic comedy 'NON-REFUNDABLE'. Filming is scheduled from November 30, 2026, to February 18, 2027.

The film follows a broken-up couple who are still financially obligated to pay for their destination wedding venue. Grudgingly, they both show up to the Mexican location, each bringing their new partners along to try to one-up the other.

#TheAltruists, starring Emmy winner Julia Garner, is NOW STREAMING on Netflix!

"The story of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, two hyper-smart, ambitious young idealists who tried to remake the global financial system in the blink of an eye - before they were accused of stealing $8 billion and became Gen Z's own Bonnie & Clyde."

Netflix has officially set a release date for its upcoming adult animated sitcom, Living the Dream. Created by BAFTA-nominated George Gendi, the show follows two friends working at a London-based "save-the-planet" company called Ecofood.

The series is being described as a spiritual successor to Gendi's previous hit, 'Apple & Onion,' but with a more mature, grounded workplace setting.

'The Inbetweeners 3' has officially finished filming! The boys have spent the last seven weeks shooting across the UK and Spain, with stars Joe Thomas and James Buckley now sharing the first behind-the-scenes details from the set.

From a massive church wedding in Surrey to the familiar beaches of Magaluf, we have tracked every filming location for the gang's long-awaited return.

प्रविधिको क्षेत्रमा उत्तर कोरियाले नयाँ उपलब्धि सार्वजनिक गरेको छ। लामो समयदेखि अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय प्रतिबन्ध र प्रविधिमा सीमित पहुँचको सामना गरिरहेको उत्तर कोरियाले आफ्नै आर्टिफिसियल इन्टेलिजेन्स (एआई) च्याटबट प्रदर्शन गरेको हो।

अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय समाचार संस्था रोयटर्सका अनुसार उत्तर कोरियाले एक प्रविधि प्रदर्शनीमा एआई च्याटबट देखाएको छ। उत्तर कोरियासम्बन्धी अनुसन्धान गर्ने संस्था ‘३८ नर्थ’ ले सरकारी टेलिभिजनमा प्रसारित दृश्यहरूको अध्ययन गर्दै देशले सम्भवतः आफ्नो पहिलो एआई च्याटबट विकास गरेको जनाएको छ।

यो च्याटबटले कोरियाली र अंग्रेजी भाषामा विज्ञान तथा प्रविधिसम्बन्धी प्रश्नहरूको जवाफ दिन सक्ने बताइएको छ। किम इल सुङ विश्वविद्यालयसँग सम्बन्धित अनुसन्धानकर्ताहरूले यसको विकासमा भूमिका खेलेको विवरण सार्वजनिक भएको छ।

अमेरिका र चीनबीच एआई प्रविधिमा तीव्र प्रतिस्पर्धा चलिरहेका बेला उत्तर कोरियाले पनि आफ्नो प्रविधि प्रदर्शन गर्नुलाई महत्त्वपूर्ण घटनाका रूपमा हेरिएको छ। यद्यपि यसको क्षमता, विश्वसनीयता र सर्वसाधारणका लागि उपलब्धताबारे थप विवरण आउन बाँकी छ।

कुनै बेला नेपालजस्तै गरिब दक्षिण कोरियाको विकासले दुनियाँ चकित! एक वर्षमै १ ट्रिलियन डलरभन्दा बढीको निर्यात!

कुनै समय युद्ध र गरिबीले थलिएको दक्षिण कोरियाले आर्थिक विकासमा नयाँ इतिहास रचेको छ। सन् २०२६ को एक वर्ष पूरा नहुँदै दक्षिण कोरियाले **१ ट्रिलियन अमेरिकी डलर अर्थात् १० खर्ब डलरभन्दा बढीको वस्तु निर्यात** गरेर विश्वलाई चकित पारेको छ।

दक्षिण कोरियाको उद्योग तथा व्यापार मन्त्रालयका अनुसार नोभेम्बर १९ मा देशको कुल निर्यातले पहिलोपटक १ ट्रिलियन डलरको ऐतिहासिक सीमा पार गरेको हो। यो उपलब्धिसँगै दक्षिण कोरिया चीन, अमेरिका र जर्मनीपछि एक वर्षमा १ ट्रिलियन डलरभन्दा बढीको निर्यात गर्ने विश्वको चौथो राष्ट्र बनेको छ।

दक्षिण कोरियाले सन् २०२५ को पूरा वर्षमा करिब ७१० अर्ब डलरको निर्यात गरेको थियो। तर यस वर्ष १२ महिना नपुग्दै उक्त कीर्तिमान तोडिएको छ।

यस ऐतिहासिक सफलतामा सेमिकन्डक्टर चिप, आर्टिफिसियल इन्टेलिजेन्स (AI) सम्बन्धी प्रविधि, विद्युतीय उपकरण, गाडी तथा अन्य औद्योगिक उत्पादनको महत्वपूर्ण योगदान रहेको छ।

कुनै समय गरिबी र विनाशको सामना गरेको दक्षिण कोरियाले शिक्षा, प्रविधि, उद्योग र अनुसन्धानमा गरेको लगानीमार्फत आज विश्व अर्थतन्त्रमा आफ्नो बलियो स्थान बनाएको छ।

नेपालमा बन्ने भयो करिब १,००० किलोमिटर लामो हिमाली पर्यटकीय राजमार्ग! पहिलो चरणको अध्ययन सुरु!

नेपालको पर्यटन र पूर्वाधार विकासमा नयाँ आयाम थप्ने उद्देश्यले सरकारले विशाल पूर्व–पश्चिम हिमाली पर्यटकीय राजमार्ग निर्माणको योजना अघि बढाएको छ। देशका पूर्वदेखि पश्चिमसम्मका प्रमुख हिमाली पर्यटकीय गन्तव्यलाई एउटै सडक सञ्जालमा जोड्ने लक्ष्य राखिएको छ।

प्रस्तावित राजमार्गको लम्बाइ करिब ८४४ देखि १,००० किलोमिटर हुने प्रारम्भिक अनुमान छ। पहिलो चरणमा १५० किलोमिटर सडकको सम्भाव्यता अध्ययनका लागि सडक विभाग र नेपाल पूर्वाधार निर्माण कम्पनीबीच सम्झौता भएको छ।

यसअन्तर्गत दार्चुलाको अपिनाम्पादेखि बझाङको सैपाल हुँदै बाजुराको बडीमालिकासम्म १०५ किलोमिटर र संखुवासभाको नुमदेखि ताप्लेजुङको पाथीभरासम्म ४५ किलोमिटर सडकको अध्ययन गरिनेछ।

आयोजना निर्माण सम्पन्न भएमा दुर्गम हिमाली बस्तीमा यातायात पहुँच विस्तार हुनुका साथै पर्यटन, व्यापार र स्थानीय रोजगारीका अवसर बढ्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

यद्यपि राजमार्ग अहिले सम्भाव्यता अध्ययनकै चरणमा रहेकाले निर्माण सुरु हुने मिति र अन्तिम लम्बाइ तय हुन बाँकी छ।

ताइवान आसपास चीनले ठूलो सैन्य उपस्थिति देखाएको छ। ताइवानका सुरक्षा अधिकारीहरूका अनुसार चीनले पश्चिमी प्रशान्त क्षेत्रमा १०० भन्दा बढी नौसेना र तटरक्षक जहाज परिचालन गर्दै सैन्य गतिविधि तीव्र बनाएको हो।

बिहान ८:४५ देखि ९:४५ बजेसम्म काठमाडौंको वायु गुणस्तर सूचकांक (AQI) १८३ पुगेको थियो। पाकिस्तानको लाहोर ३२५ सहित पहिलो र बंगलादेशको ढाका २५६ सहित दोस्रो स्थानमा रहेका थिए।

विज्ञहरूले प्रदूषण उच्च भएका बेला अनावश्यक रूपमा बाहिर ननिस्कन, बाहिर निस्कँदा एन९५ मास्क प्रयोग गर्न र स्वास्थ्यको विशेष ख्याल राख्न सुझाव दिएका छन्।

Once operational, the airport could also contribute to Nepal's tourism sector, international trade, regional connectivity and employment opportunities, while supporting the country's broader infrastructure and economic development ambitions.

The government's planned decision on the construction model by mid-December is expected to be a key step toward determining how the long-awaited airport project will proceed.

Keiko, the killer whale who starred in the movie *Free Willy*, spent nearly 23 years in captivity before being released into Icelandic waters in 2002.

A MAJOR LEGAL MILESTONE IN THE PROTECTION OF ORCAS. 🐋

California's Orca Protection Act, enacted in 2016, made it illegal to breed or impregnate captive orcas in the state. It also prohibits keeping orcas for display, performance, or entertainment, with an exception for orcas already held in captivity before January 1, 2017.

Those existing orcas may continue to be held and used in qualifying educational presentations, but breeding is prohibited.

Anyone who intentionally or negligently violates the law can face misdemeanor charges and a fine of up to $100,000.

The law does not immediately release captive orcas, but it prevents future breeding and establishes important restrictions on their captivity.

Source: California Fish and Game Code, Section 4502.5 — California Orca Protection Act.

A CLOSE ENCOUNTER THAT REVEALED THE HIDDEN DANGERS OF OCEAN POLLUTION. 🐋

In 2024, wildlife guide Lorien Cleavinger encountered a female sperm whale in the Indian Ocean with floating trash and plant debris caught in its mouth and throat.

While other swimmers filmed, Cleavinger carefully removed pieces of debris with her bare hands. According to her account, the whale remained relatively still throughout the encounter and stayed near the group afterward.

She later reported seeing the same whale again, appearing healthy and hunting with its pod.

Although the encounter had a positive outcome, approaching or touching wild whales is extremely dangerous for both people and animals. This remarkable moment also reminds us how marine pollution can affect even the ocean's largest creatures.

A REMARKABLE NEW CHAPTER IN AN ORCA FAMILY'S HISTORY. 🐋

In March 2025, researchers documented a new Bigg’s killer whale calf, T046B3A, in the Salish Sea. The calf belongs to a family descended from the Budd Inlet Six, a group of orcas captured in Washington in 1976.

Public pressure helped secure the release of six whales, with Ralph Munro among those who fought for their freedom. One female, later named Wake, was not released and remained in captivity.

In an extraordinary coincidence, Munro died on March 20, 2025—the same day the calf's arrival was announced. The young whale represents the continuation of a family line that survived a defining moment in orca conservation history.

Source: Smithsonian Magazine

The real story: On October 7, 2026, two juvenile humpback whales were found stuck on sandbars off Fire Island, New York. The U.S. Coast Guard helped respond, and both whales returned to open water as the tide rose. Source: ABC7 New York and News 12 Long Island, published October 8, 2026.

Two young humpback whales ran into trouble off Fire Island, New York, on October 7, 2026: both had become stuck on sandbars, in water too shallow to swim in. A stranded whale is in a race against the tide, because its body isn't built to be out of the water's support, and every hour on the sand increases the risk.

The U.S. Coast Guard responded to help rescue the juvenile humpbacks, and crews monitored both animals as the water began to rise. Local reports described the outcome as a happy one: the tide came in, the whales were freed, and both swam back out to sea.

It was a rare piece of good news in a season that has brought several whale strandings to the Northeast. The most important part of such a rescue, according to marine mammal responders, is what the public does and doesn't do: call the Coast Guard or a stranding network right away, stay back, and let trained responders decide whether to help or to let the tide do the work.

“AMBUSHED ON A 100-FOOT MOUNTAIN. HE SCALED THE VERTICAL ICE WALL UNDER MACHINE-GUN FIRE.” — The Heroism of Green Beret Matthew Williams.

On April 6, 2008, during Operation Commando Wrath in eastern Afghanistan’s jagged Shok Valley, Green Beret Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336) and Afghan Commandos inserted into an insurgent stronghold perched atop a 100-foot near-vertical cliff.

As the lead assault force climbed the mountain, over 200 fortified fighters opened up from terraced caves and ridges with heavy machine guns, sniper fire, and RPGs—trapping the lead element on an exposed ledge with multiple critical casualties:

• Charging Through the Crossfire: Realizing his teammates were in danger of being overrun, Sergeant Matthew Williams gathered a team of commandos and charged across a 100-meter kill zone of ice-covered boulders and a freezing, waist-deep river under concentrated enemy fire.

• Scaling the 100-Foot Wall: Facing a near-vertical cliff of jagged ice and rock, Williams climbed straight up the mountain face while enemy rounds ricocheted off the rock inches from his hands to reach his besieged teammates.

• Evacuating the Wounded: When his team sergeant, Master Sgt. Scott Ford, was shot by sniper fire, Williams rendered field first aid under continuous fire, then helped lower Ford and other wounded soldiers down the sheer 100-foot drop to the casualty collection point.

• Climbing Back Up Into the Fight: Refusing to stay in safety, Williams scaled the cliff face a second time under relentless fire to defend the remaining isolated team members and recover four more critically wounded soldiers.

In six hours of brutal, high-altitude mountain combat, Williams repeatedly exposed himself to enemy fire to direct air strikes and guide in medevac helicopters. Every wounded American survived.

On October 30, 2019, President Donald Trump presented the Medal of Honor to Master Sergeant Matthew O. Williams, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave his teammates on that mountain.

Scaling a 100-foot vertical cliff under machine-gun fire, lowering your wounded brothers down, and then climbing straight back up into the firefight—what does Matthew Williams’ courage tell you about the standard of America’s Special Forces?

“A STUDENT DROPPED A LIVE GRENADE IN THE PIT: THIS MARINE PUT HIS BODY IN FRONT OF THE BLAST.”

You have three seconds before a live fragmentation grenade detonates. On a live-fire training range at Camp Pendleton, a terrified student lost his grip. Staff Sergeant Brett Meil didn't hesitate—he shoved the young Marine behind him and placed his own torso directly in the line of the blast.

On June 13, 2023, then-Sergeant Brett D. Meil was serving as the position safety officer on the live-fire grenade range at the School of Infantry – West (SOI-West).

When a student inadvertently released the safety lever inside the throwing pit, activating the live M67 fuse, fear took over and the student froze. Recognizing the imminent explosion, Meil took immediate action:

Clearing the Pit: Meil forcibly wrestled the grenade away and threw both himself and the student out of the pit to escape the confined blast pressure.

The Fatal Ricochet: The grenade bounced off an interior bunker wall and rolled outside the pit, landing mere feet away on the dirt right next to the two Marines.

Becoming a Human Shield: With less than two seconds remaining, Meil grabbed the student, pulled the young Marine tight against his chest, and wrapped his entire body over him to absorb the blast.

Absorbing the Shrapnel: The grenade detonated, showering Meil with hundreds of high-velocity fragments. He took the brunt of the explosion across his back and limbs, saving the student, who walked away with only minor injuries.

Assessing His Marine First: Despite catastrophic wounds and intense bleeding, Meil’s first action was checking his student’s condition and calling for immediate medical support before allowing corpsmen to treat his own trauma.

On September 24, 2024, at Camp Pendleton, Colonel Patrick B. Byrne presented Staff Sergeant Brett D. Meil with the Navy and Marine Corps Medal—the Department of the Navy’s highest non-combat decoration for heroism.

“Staff Sgt. Meil performed exactly the way that we ask combat instructors to,” said Col. Byrne. “He identified that there was a dangerous situation, he assessed it and immediately acted exactly appropriately to address the danger and protect the student.”

For Meil, the instinct was immediate:

“My secondary thought was the grenade's outside the pit and pulling him as close and tight to me as possible.”

Gebhard "Geb" Galle has passed away at 105, the last living crew member of the USS Nevada, the only battleship to get underway during the attack on Pearl Harbor.

On December 7, 1941, he was below deck waiting to go ashore for church when the explosions started. "We felt a couple jolts, and that's when we got hit with the torpedo," he recalled. Afterward, he saw the capsized Oklahoma and the burning Arizona. "A pretty sad lookout."

A year later, as his next ship went down at Tassafaronga, he heard someone trapped behind a locked hatch and opened it against a direct order. "Come on, get out of there. That equipment can run without you," he shouted. "I disobeyed orders," he said later. About 40 men survived in life rafts.

He served to the end of the war. Only about a dozen Pearl Harbor survivors remain.

Rest easy, sailor.

“AMBUSHED ON A 100-FOOT MOUNTAIN. HE SCALED THE VERTICAL ICE WALL UNDER MACHINE-GUN FIRE.” — The Heroism of Green Beret Matthew Williams.

On April 6, 2008, during Operation Commando Wrath in eastern Afghanistan’s jagged Shok Valley, Green Beret Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336) and Afghan Commandos inserted into an insurgent stronghold perched atop a 100-foot near-vertical cliff.

As the lead assault force climbed the mountain, over 200 fortified fighters opened up from terraced caves and ridges with heavy machine guns, sniper fire, and RPGs—trapping the lead element on an exposed ledge with multiple critical casualties:

• Charging Through the Crossfire: Realizing his teammates were in danger of being overrun, Sergeant Matthew Williams gathered a team of commandos and charged across a 100-meter kill zone of ice-covered boulders and a freezing, waist-deep river under concentrated enemy fire.

• Scaling the 100-Foot Wall: Facing a near-vertical cliff of jagged ice and rock, Williams climbed straight up the mountain face while enemy rounds ricocheted off the rock inches from his hands to reach his besieged teammates.

• Evacuating the Wounded: When his team sergeant, Master Sgt. Scott Ford, was shot by sniper fire, Williams rendered field first aid under continuous fire, then helped lower Ford and other wounded soldiers down the sheer 100-foot drop to the casualty collection point.

• Climbing Back Up Into the Fight: Refusing to stay in safety, Williams scaled the cliff face a second time under relentless fire to defend the remaining isolated team members and recover four more critically wounded soldiers.

In six hours of brutal, high-altitude mountain combat, Williams repeatedly exposed himself to enemy fire to direct air strikes and guide in medevac helicopters. Every wounded American survived.

On October 30, 2019, President Donald Trump presented the Medal of Honor to Master Sergeant Matthew O. Williams, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave his teammates on that mountain.

Scaling a 100-foot vertical cliff under machine-gun fire, lowering your wounded brothers down, and then climbing straight back up into the firefight—what does Matthew Williams’ courage tell you about the standard of America’s Special Forces?

“A STUDENT DROPPED A LIVE GRENADE IN THE PIT: THIS MARINE PUT HIS BODY IN FRONT OF THE BLAST.”

You have three seconds before a live fragmentation grenade detonates. On a live-fire training range at Camp Pendleton, a terrified student lost his grip. Staff Sergeant Brett Meil didn't hesitate—he shoved the young Marine behind him and placed his own torso directly in the line of the blast.

On June 13, 2023, then-Sergeant Brett D. Meil was serving as the position safety officer on the live-fire grenade range at the School of Infantry – West (SOI-West).

When a student inadvertently released the safety lever inside the throwing pit, activating the live M67 fuse, fear took over and the student froze. Recognizing the imminent explosion, Meil took immediate action:

Clearing the Pit: Meil forcibly wrestled the grenade away and threw both himself and the student out of the pit to escape the confined blast pressure.

The Fatal Ricochet: The grenade bounced off an interior bunker wall and rolled outside the pit, landing mere feet away on the dirt right next to the two Marines.

Becoming a Human Shield: With less than two seconds remaining, Meil grabbed the student, pulled the young Marine tight against his chest, and wrapped his entire body over him to absorb the blast.

Absorbing the Shrapnel: The grenade detonated, showering Meil with hundreds of high-velocity fragments. He took the brunt of the explosion across his back and limbs, saving the student, who walked away with only minor injuries.

Assessing His Marine First: Despite catastrophic wounds and intense bleeding, Meil’s first action was checking his student’s condition and calling for immediate medical support before allowing corpsmen to treat his own trauma.

On September 24, 2024, at Camp Pendleton, Colonel Patrick B. Byrne presented Staff Sergeant Brett D. Meil with the Navy and Marine Corps Medal—the Department of the Navy’s highest non-combat decoration for heroism.

“Staff Sgt. Meil performed exactly the way that we ask combat instructors to,” said Col. Byrne. “He identified that there was a dangerous situation, he assessed it and immediately acted exactly appropriately to address the danger and protect the student.”

For Meil, the instinct was immediate:

“My secondary thought was the grenade's outside the pit and pulling him as close and tight to me as possible.”

 Swimming against powerful currents, he towed the victims through the swells to within 25 meters of the vessel, secured a heavy safety line, and hauled them safely aboard before ensuring everyone was accounted for on the return to port.

74 years ago today, one American pilot took on seven Soviet MiGs… alone. 

November 18, 1952.
Navy Lieutenant Royce Williams was flying an F9F Panther off the coast of Korea when he suddenly found himself facing seven Soviet MiG-15s.

Outnumbered.
Outmatched in speed and climb.
And completely alone.

For 35 minutes — the longest dogfight in U.S. Navy history — Williams fought them.
He shot down four of the Soviet jets.
His plane was hit by a 37mm cannon shell, hydraulics failing, yet he still made it back to the carrier and landed.

Because the enemy pilots were Soviet (not North Korean or Chinese), the entire engagement was classified.
Williams was ordered to keep quiet.
He did — for more than 50 years.

Only after the Cold War ended did the full story come out.
In February of this year, at age 100, he finally received the Medal of Honor.
He is now 101.

One man.
Seven enemy jets.
Four confirmed kills.
And a secret kept for half a century.

Some stories still stop you cold.

High-altitude mountain rescue leaves zero room for error. When a catastrophic fall in the Colorado backcountry left a Green Beret paralyzed and freezing, Sergeant First Class Bobby Haran stabilized the traumatic injuries, rigged a descent system, and hauled his teammate down a sheer rock face to an area where a rescue chopper could touch its skids.

At the summit of the 14,023-foot Wilson Peak near Telluride, Colorado, SFC Robert "Bobby" Haran an elite mountain instructor with the Special Operations Mountain Warfare Training Center (10th Special Forces Group) watched his teammate’s lead ski strike a submerged rock, releasing the binding and triggering an uncontrolled, 2,000-foot plunge down an icy couloir.

What followed was one of the most remarkable acts of alpine mountaineering and survival in Special Operations history:

Knowing that skiing the steep route solo risked triggering massive avalanches onto his injured partner, Haran descended 2,200 vertical feet on foot across near-vertical ice using only crampons and an ice axe, hauling his teammate's recovered skis to use as an emergency litter.

Reaching his teammate, Haran found him suffering from a fractured sternum, broken hip, shattered shoulder, compound leg fractures, internal bleeding, a torn aorta, and severe hypothermia. Haran stabilized his breathing and wounds in sub-zero winds.

Communicating via emergency satellite with San Miguel County Search and Rescue, Haran rigged a lowering system and moved his paralyzed teammate hundreds of feet further down sheer rock to an improvised alpine landing zone.

After a rescue helicopter hoisted the casualty to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction, Haran skied the remaining backcountry miles solo back to the trailhead.

During a formal ceremony at Fort Carson, Major General Lawrence G. Ferguson presented the Soldier's Medal—the Army's highest peacetime decoration for heroism—to honor Haran's extraordinary valor and skill.

“Bobby, without a doubt, is the only individual that comes to mind that could have performed the way he did that day,” Haran’s NCOIC concluded. “Because of all his training, perseverance, and wherewithal, it resulted in him saving his teammate's life.”

 The 70-Foot Shot

“AMBUSHED ON A 100-FOOT MOUNTAIN. HE SCALED THE VERTICAL ICE WALL UNDER MACHINE-GUN FIRE.” — The Heroism of Green Beret Matthew Williams.

On April 6, 2008, during Operation Commando Wrath in eastern Afghanistan’s jagged Shok Valley, Green Beret Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336) and Afghan Commandos inserted into an insurgent stronghold perched atop a 100-foot near-vertical cliff.

As the lead assault force climbed the mountain, over 200 fortified fighters opened up from terraced caves and ridges with heavy machine guns, sniper fire, and RPGs—trapping the lead element on an exposed ledge with multiple critical casualties:

• Charging Through the Crossfire: Realizing his teammates were in danger of being overrun, Sergeant Matthew Williams gathered a team of commandos and charged across a 100-meter kill zone of ice-covered boulders and a freezing, waist-deep river under concentrated enemy fire.

• Scaling the 100-Foot Wall: Facing a near-vertical cliff of jagged ice and rock, Williams climbed straight up the mountain face while enemy rounds ricocheted off the rock inches from his hands to reach his besieged teammates.

• Evacuating the Wounded: When his team sergeant, Master Sgt. Scott Ford, was shot by sniper fire, Williams rendered field first aid under continuous fire, then helped lower Ford and other wounded soldiers down the sheer 100-foot drop to the casualty collection point.

• Climbing Back Up Into the Fight: Refusing to stay in safety, Williams scaled the cliff face a second time under relentless fire to defend the remaining isolated team members and recover four more critically wounded soldiers.

In six hours of brutal, high-altitude mountain combat, Williams repeatedly exposed himself to enemy fire to direct air strikes and guide in medevac helicopters. Every wounded American survived.

On October 30, 2019, President Donald Trump presented the Medal of Honor to Master Sergeant Matthew O. Williams, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave his teammates on that mountain.

Scaling a 100-foot vertical cliff under machine-gun fire, lowering your wounded brothers down, and then climbing straight back up into the firefight—what does Matthew Williams’ courage tell you about the standard of America’s Special Forces?

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along the west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush.

B-1 bomber pilots are now training in this little business jet…
and it’s giving them 100 extra flight hours a year. 

The B-1 Lancer is one of the most expensive aircraft in the Air Force inventory to fly.
Every hour in that bomber costs serious money — and those hours are limited.

So the Air Force came up with a workaround.

Near Dyess Air Force Base, B-1 pilots are now flying contractor-owned light jets (HondaJets) under a new program called BSTAR.
These smaller, much cheaper aircraft let them practice core flying skills — instrument work, handling, crew coordination — without burning through precious B-1 flight hours.

The result?
About 100 additional hours in the air each year for each participating pilot.

The expensive bomber hours stay focused on the things only a B-1 can do: aerial refueling, weapons employment, and combat tactics.

Some will say it’s a smart, cost-effective way to keep pilots sharp.
Others might wonder if training in a tiny business jet really prepares you for a 150-foot-long bomber.

Either way, the Air Force is betting that more time in the air — even in a smaller plane — is better than sitting on the ground.

Army Capt. Shaina Coss is the first woman to lead elite Army Rangers in combat.

Despite her trailblazing service, the 30-year-old from Fairfax, Virginia said in a publicly-released video that her “infantry path has been pretty typical.” After graduating from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 2016 where she competed on the powerlifting team, Coss completed Army Ranger School — one of the first 10 women to ever do so — and then moved on to Fort Bragg where she led an infantry rifle platoon in the 82nd Airborne Division. Just months into being a platoon leader, she applied to be a part of the 75th Ranger Regiment, the Army’s elite special operations force.
